$comment: S5 judge rubric ROUND 2 (methodology/05-eval-rubric.md #judge) - all 83 items scored fresh on all six dimensions by an examiner who wrote the strongest honest case FOR every distractor before scoring, and who did not open the round-1 scores until the blind solve and key diff were on disk. The reworked item (gcp-cdl-d4-10) was re-scored fresh with no partial credit, per #bounce. Result: no dimension <=2 anywhere in the bank, so ZERO rubric bounces; the round-1 overlap bounce is discharged (see overlap-report.md). Round 1 preserved at judge-scores-r1.json. Precondition note: `pnpm validate gcp-cdl` is red on this tree with 20 errors, ALL of them selection-shape / selection-format-mix because selection.json is still the empty S6 placeholder; every bank-quality check passes, so S5 proceeded on a well-formed bank.

items.case: Argued FOR: A (hybrid cloud deployment) - the board approved a cloud-enabled program, so a director reaching for a concrete noun could pick the deployment model; loses because no on-premises/public split is described and a deployment model is not an organizational change. C (the cloud) - the stem names cloud services as the enabler and many boards fuse the two; loses on the guide's own separation of the consumption model from the change it enables. D (modernized infrastructure estate) - infrastructure genuinely is being modernized; loses because it names an ingredient of the program. Dim2 3: all three wrong options are one error in three costumes (name the enabler, not the change) and C in particular is thin. Dim5 3: the stem paraphrases the definition and then asks for the word, which is recall rather than good-vs-best. Dim6 4: the tourism-board wrapper does almost no work.

Argued FOR: B (generates novel content) is the live tempter because the second tool DOES draft a firing plan, so a candidate reading 'drafts' as the discriminator lands on generative AI; loses because drafting once and stopping is a single call, not goal pursuit. A (bigger training set) is a real folk explanation of capability. C (AI infrastructure) is true of either tool. Dim5 3: the stem enumerates the multi-step pursuit ('checks... drafts... reserves... confirms') and the key restates it, so the surface points AT the principle.

Argued FOR: B (open standard) is the strongest case in the item - a technology committee protecting itself from a stalled vendor genuinely does ask for standards-based products; loses because a shared specification governs interoperability, not access to the vendor's source. C (multicloud) is a real lock-in safeguard about where the product runs. D (published APIs) opens the integration layer only. Dim2 5: three distinct, live commitments a real committee would table. Dim5 4: the inspect-and-modify requirement points fairly directly at source access, but B is close enough to keep the discrimination honest.

Argued FOR: A (cost-effectiveness) is the CFO's instinct and true of cloud generally - servers sized for a peak that happens twice a year are wasted money; loses because the stated pain is a site that fails, not a bill that is too high. B (agility) answers slow change. D (permanent peak capacity) is the wrong-lever option and a real board proposal. Dim2 4: D is a policy rather than a cloud property, which makes it slightly off-pattern. Dim5 4: the surface points at capacity, but three of the four options are true cloud benefits, so choosing the one that addresses the failure mode is a leader-level judgment rather than a match.

Argued FOR: C (offsite backups) is the strongest wrong case - a board that has just lost a portal for a day thinks about recovery, and backups are what recovery usually means; loses because a backup restores after an outage rather than serving through one, and it moves nothing closer to users abroad. D (pay-as-you-go) is a real benefit at the wrong address. B (more total capacity) is disarmed by the stem's own 'beyond more machines' clause and can be eliminated without engaging the concept - that caps dim2 at 3. Dim5 4: the two symptoms in the stem (slow from abroad, one long outage) point at reach and availability, but A vs C still needs the distinction.

Argued FOR: B (near-unlimited seasonal capacity) is a genuine cloud benefit and the one a garden centre feels most; loses because the CIO explicitly asked for benefits that are not about capacity. D (paying only for what each store consumes) is the same exclusion on the cost axis. E (provider takes over compliance obligations) is the factually false option and the only one that fails on its own terms. Dim2 3: two of the three wrong options are eliminated by the stem's own exclusion clause rather than by the concept. Dim6 4: the CFO/CIO framing is plausible but the setting does little work beyond supplying the exclusion.

Argued FOR: A (a high-profile AI launch) is exactly how transformation programs actually get proposed, and 'newest is best' is a real boardroom argument; loses because it is news about technology with no customer or competitive pressure attached. B (regional availability) is an enabler mistaken for a driver. C (unspent budget) is a real organizational behaviour and a famously bad reason. Dim2 4: C is a weaker practitioner answer than the other two. Dim5 4: the rival's halved turnaround is a clear signal, but all four options are things leadership teams really say.

Argued FOR: A (peak volume) - performance hurdles are the usual suspect when a program stalls; loses because the stem states the platform performs well in every test, so A is contradicted rather than outargued. C (wrong deployment model) and D (licensing budget) have no support in the scenario at all. Dim2 3: one option is disarmed by the stem's own wording and the other two are unsupported filler rather than real practitioner answers. Dim5 4: crews filing paper against a working system points at people, but the candidate still has to name the hurdle class.

Argued FOR: B (only a delay) is the strongest case and is precisely what the board minutes assert - the same benefits will be there later; loses because competitors' gains and legacy drift compound, so the later move closes a wider gap. C (a genuine reduction in spend) is what 'prudent cost avoidance' means to a finance committee. D (retraining avoided) names a real cost of adopting. Dim2 4: D answers the wrong side of the decision and is the weakest of the three. Dim5 4: the stem describes competitors widening the lead, which points at the answer without handing over the compounding framing.

Argued FOR: A (world-leading AI models) is a real Google differentiator and the obvious pick for anything called an AI roadmap; loses because model quality does nothing for records that are not yet usable as input. B (AI Hypercomputer) is the infrastructure sibling on the same list and a genuine tempter. D (prestige) is not a differentiator at all. Dim2 4: D is decorative next to A and B. Dim5 4: matching the differentiator to the stakeholder's stated concern is real good-vs-best work, but 'without rebuilding the data estate' points fairly directly.

Argued FOR: A (multicloud) is the term most often misused for exactly this arrangement; loses because multicloud means two or more public providers, not provider-plus-own-facilities. D (public cloud with residency settings) is the subtle one - a leader may believe residency controls satisfy a facilities clause; loses because residency chooses where inside the provider's estate the data sits. C (private for everything) satisfies the licence and surrenders the elasticity. Dim2 4: C is a half-answer rather than a distinct misconception. Dim5 4: the split is stated plainly, so the mapping is direct, but D is a genuine trap.

Argued FOR: A (the swap) is the real trap - candidates who half-remember the pair get the direction wrong; loses on the definitions. C (a firewall translates the name) is a live confusion for non-engineers. B (bandwidth decides the server) is the weakest. Dim5 3: this is textbook recall of what DNS does, with no misdirection in the surface. Dim6 4: the toll-operator wrapper is scenery rather than scenario.

Argued FOR: B (bandwidth) is the intended trap and a real one, since the stem mentions large uploads and volume language pulls toward throughput; loses because those uploads finishing quickly is the evidence that clears bandwidth. C (storage capacity) is a plausible layperson answer for 'sluggish'. D (deployment model) is thin. Dim2 4: D is filler next to B. Dim5 4: the two-signal design (slow clicks, fast bulk) is genuine discrimination work.

Argued FOR: A (zones are collections of regions) is the inversion trap and the answer a candidate who has the words but not the nesting gives. B (availability districts) is an invented tier that sounds official. D (a region is one building) is the flattening misconception. Dim2 4: B is eliminable by anyone who knows the vocabulary at all. Dim5 3: this is recall of the geography hierarchy; the briefing wrapper adds no misdirection. Dim6 4: the leasing-firm setting does little work.

Argued FOR: A (IaaS) is one rung away and the strongest case - a library that controls an application on provisioned servers can feel like an IaaS tenant; loses because the provider patches the OS and runtime here. C (SaaS) is where the library would consume a finished product. D (serverless) is the category error a reader who knows compute but not service models makes. Dim2 5: three distinct, real misreadings. Dim5 4: the responsibility boundary is stated cleanly, which makes the mapping direct but not free.

Argued FOR: B (timelier reporting from an hourly rerun) is the strongest wrong case and what most operations teams actually do; loses because between runs the control room is still reading history. A (identifying trends) is a genuine value of the same data on a seasonal horizon. D (fueling AI) is real and postponed. Dim5 5: all four options are true values of data, and the discriminator is whether the answer expires - the surface points away from the principle.

Argued FOR: B (data warehouse) is the live tempter because the analysts already query with SQL and most of the volume is structured; loses because accreditation requires native retention of scans and traces. C (warehouse plus file share) is what most labs really do. D (governance) is real work aimed at a different question. Dim5 5: the majority-volume and SQL cues point at the warehouse, so the surface misdirects.

Argued FOR: A (second-party) is the strongest case - the developer does have a direct commercial relationship with the seller, which is what second-party usually means; loses because the seller collected none of the data. C (brokered data) is an invented class that sounds like a real register category. D (first-party via licence) misreads ownership. Dim2 4: C is invented and eliminable by vocabulary alone. Dim5 4: the aggregator description points at the answer, but A is a genuine misread of 'directly'.

Argued FOR: A (collection) is defensible if the reader treats the whole intake pipeline as one stage. B (governance) is the answer for who may alter a label and a real confusion because quality rules feel like governance. C (activation) is the design many teams end up with, mapping codes per report. Dim2 5: three real stages, each a genuine misassignment. Dim5 4: the described work is textbook processing, so the mapping is fairly direct.

Argued FOR: A (a data quality tool) is the IT manager's own proposal and it does address the duplicate and stale records; loses because nothing stops the defects returning while no one owns the recall list. B (a data lake) preserves both versions and settles nothing. D (encryption) is a control aimed outside the group when the spreadsheet is circulating inside it. Dim5 5: the surface offers a tool and the principle is governance - real misdirection.

Argued FOR: C (copies drifting apart) is the strongest wrong case, since divergent exports are exactly what the partners have lived through; loses because drift is a symptom silos produce rather than the failure mode openness names. A (outage access) is an availability concern answered by replication. D (format decay) is an invented term dressed as canonical. Dim1 holds because select-two forces the two named modes and C is subsumed by B. Dim5 4: the export-only tooling points at lock-in, but C keeps the choice live.

Argued FOR: D (Cloud SQL with read replicas) is the strongest case and the architecture most teams reach for; loses because every write still lands in one region, which is the sharding the agency refuses. B (Bigtable) is a real scale answer with no relational transactions. A (BigQuery) is where reservation history is analyzed. Dim5 5: three of the four are products a practitioner would defend, and the discriminator is global write consistency.

Argued FOR: C (accounts and catalog both relational) is the strongest case - many teams do force variable attributes into one schema with nullable columns; loses because per-category attributes are the constraint non-relational models exist to lift. D inverts the accounts assignment. A (all non-relational) is the weakest, resting on a wrong definition. Dim2 4: A is thin next to C. Dim5 4: three workloads described by their shape make the mapping direct, though C is genuinely arguable.

Argued FOR: B (Nearline) is the designed near-miss and the answer of a candidate who knows the classes exist but not their frequency bands; loses because once or twice a decade is far below monthly. A (Standard) is the availability instinct and defensible if retrieval latency worried the practice. C (match the other buckets) is a real billing-hygiene habit. Dim2 4: C is an operational habit rather than a storage answer. Dim5 5: the Nearline/Archive discrimination is the good-vs-best core of the item.

Argued FOR: C (Standard until the pattern is understood) is the strongest wrong case and standard advice in most teams; loses because the operator has said the pattern will keep shifting, so the review never ends. B (monthly reviews) is the half-measure that keeps the manual loop. D (Archive everything) is the cheapest-rate trap. Dim5 5: the surface offers a sensible-sounding manual policy and the principle is to stop guessing.

Argued FOR: A (refactor) is what a modernization-minded board would want and it does lift the vendor constraint; loses because the vendor will not certify a change and there are no developers. B (retain) is defensible right up to the point that support ended three years ago. D (analytics product) is a real product mismatch. Dim5 4: the constraints are stated explicitly, so the elimination is clean, though every option is a real migration decision.

Argued FOR: A (a warehouse) is genuinely useful and is what most consultants would propose first; loses because consolidation changes nothing about who can ask a question. C (grant table access) is the IT answer and fails on capability rather than permission. D (a second analyst) is what the budget holder suggests. Dim5 5: three plausible programs of work, and the discriminator is self-service on governed figures.

Argued FOR: C (on-demand refresh, booking system unchanged) is the strongest wrong case because it is true as far as it goes - a direct connection does remove the day-old extract; loses on the stem's second complaint, that managers must leave the booking system at all. B (hourly copies) preserves the design that creates staleness. A (storage cost) answers a complaint nobody made. Dim1 holds: C is true-but-partial under the E07 pattern, and the key answers both complaints. Dim5 5.

Argued FOR: C (hourly rerun) is the strongest wrong case and the cheapest thing an operator can actually do; loses because a fall still waits for the next run. B (trustees' pack) and D (weekly quality review) are real reporting needs with no expiry. Dim5 4: a fall alarm is an obvious streaming case, so the surface points at the principle, but the three reporting foils are well chosen.

Argued FOR: A (Dataflow) is the strongest case by far - it is the neighbouring stage, it does handle each reading, and many readers treat 'streaming' and 'Dataflow' as synonyms; loses because pointing meters at a processing pipeline leaves nothing decoupling publishers from consumers. B (file export) and D (direct connections) are the two architectures the firm is trying to escape. Dim5 5: the adjacent-product trap is exactly the good-vs-best pitch.

Argued FOR: D (both are machine learning) is the strongest wrong case and is defensible on its face, since generative models are built with machine learning; it loses only on the question asked - the board wants the term that distinguishes the two, and D collapses it. A (both generative) stretches the newer branch over a prediction. C (no labelled data, so no ML) is a real half-memory. Dim1 4, not 5: D is true-but-incomplete rather than wrong, so the key wins on best-answer convention rather than on D's own collapse - worth a Gate 2 eye if the deep-read disagrees with the E07 reading. Dim5 4.

Argued FOR: B (the dashboard) is the intended trap and a real one, since explaining why margins fell feels like generating an account. A (both) rests on the same conflation. C (neither, because the models are licensed) is the weakest - provenance says nothing about function. Dim2 4: C is thin. Dim5 4: the two-tool contrast is clean, so the mapping is fairly direct once the definition is held.

Argued FOR: C (operations) is the strongest wrong case because the agent really does touch scheduling and stock systems; loses because those systems are consulted, not reshaped. B (workforce productivity) is the answer if any person still finished the work, and the stem says none did. D (sales experiences) picks out the goodwill credit. Dim5 5: every option names a function the same technology genuinely transforms, and the surface points at operations.

Argued FOR: D (all-in-one AI developer platform) is the strongest case - it is the advantage most cited for building assistants, and a chief executive reading the list would land there; loses because the marketplace has nobody to build with. A (first-party models) answers what the assistant could do. B (best infrastructure) answers serving speed. Dim5 4: 'no data scientists, spring campaign' is a fairly direct cue, but all four are real claims from the same list.

Argued FOR: E (confirmation emails) is the strongest wrong case because automation is routinely sold as AI, and volume makes it feel like a scaling problem; loses because the rule is one line with nothing to learn. C (retaining five years of history) is a genuine prerequisite mistaken for the problem. B (choosing between two providers) is a commercial judgment with no pattern. Dim5 4: the two keys are recognisable, but E is a real trap for a head of operations.

Argued FOR: A (consistency) is the strongest case and a genuinely arguable one - four differently spelled titles do look like records that disagree; loses because they do not contradict each other, there are simply too many. C (timeliness) misreads accumulation over years as currency. B is the problem: it is a defended negative that argues uniqueness applies only to identical duplicates, which both telegraphs the keyed dimension and is self-defeating once read - dim2 3. Dim5 4: A keeps the discrimination alive.

Argued FOR: A (the trial settles it) is a strong commercial case and exactly what the director argues - a model that outperforms the quality team on accuracy has earned its place; loses because accuracy is not defensibility. D (review rejections afterwards) is a real governance compromise that fails on the same unexplainable score. C (publish a notice) is honest and leaves the dispute unresolved. Dim5 5: the surface offers strong trial evidence and the principle is explainability.

Argued FOR: C (volume no human could write) is the strongest wrong case, since scale is what most reviewers flinch at; loses because scale alone is not illegitimacy and practice dialogues have an obvious purpose. B and D both keep an accountable human in the loop, which is the arrangement responsible use asks for. Dim5 4: fabricated reviews under invented student names is a recognisable refusal, though the three near-misses are well built.

Argued FOR: A (implementation speed) is the default instinct and would dominate if any date existed - the stem removes it. B (technical expertise) is the constraint for most organizations and is removed by the two data scientists. D (development effort) is the budget instinct. Dim5 5: each factor is disarmed by a specific stem fact rather than by wording, which is the good-vs-best shape.

Argued FOR: A (Gemini) is the strongest case because the teams are already calling it and a model does supply the capability; loses because a model is not a place to govern what is built with it. C (Agent Registry) is an invented name that reads plausibly and would list the problem rather than solve it. B (Looker) answers governed reporting. Dim2 4: C is eliminable on vocabulary. Dim5 4: 'build, deploy and govern' points fairly directly at the platform.

Argued FOR: C (AutoML transcription) is the strongest wrong case - a trust with three thousand hours of domain audio could believe its material needs a custom model; loses because transcription is a solved task and there is nobody to train one. B (Translation API) needs text to start from. D (Cloud Storage) makes tapes playable, not searchable. Dim5 3: 'spoken words available as searchable text' is a direct modality match with no misdirection in the surface.

Argued FOR: D (a severity classifier) is the strongest case because severity is one of the four outputs and a trained classifier is the classical answer; loses because it leaves the reading, the inferred cause and the drafted summary undone. C (Translation) is a real downstream need. A (Vision API) is disarmed by the stem's 'typed' notes. Dim2 4: A is eliminable on one word of the stem. Dim5 4: the four-part job points at general generative capability.

Argued FOR: B (Vision API) is the strongest wrong case and a genuine practitioner error - it is pre-trained, needs no ML skills, and reads images; loses because it has never seen this firm's damage grades. A (Agent Studio) is the low-code route for a different job shape. C (hire an ML engineer) is real capability and more machinery than needed. Dim5 5: the pre-trained-versus-custom line is exactly the pitch, and the surface points at the easy API.

Argued FOR: D (a fixed annual allocation) is the strongest case because growers think in seasonal purchase commitments; loses because buying capacity is not what the layer is. A (a private region) describes placement. B (a managed warehouse) is the data platform layer, and a genuine confusion for a business audience. Dim2 4: D is a purchasing arrangement rather than a product-role swap. Dim5 4: 'why not simply a bigger machine' cues the integrated-stack answer.

Argued FOR: B (AutoML after exporting) is the strongest case and would be right in most organizations; loses on the stated constraint that the warehouse may not be copied. C (Looker) charts what happened. D (a manual report) is the status quo. Dim2 4: D is weak next to B. Dim5 4: SQL-only analysts plus a no-copy rule point clearly, but B is a genuine trap for anyone skimming the constraint.

Argued FOR: A (least critical first) is real migration practice and gives the board visible progress; loses because nobody knows what the least critical servers are load-bearing for. D (give a date, refine later) is exactly what happens under board pressure. B (one path for everything) is a defensible standardization instinct. Dim5 4: three of the four are things organizations really do, though the missing inventory points hard at discovery.

Argued FOR: D (retain) is the strongest wrong case and is correct until the lease date is read - keeping the system in place is legitimate right up to that boundary. B (replatform) is tempting because modest improvements sound harmless. C (refactor) is the right long-run answer with the wrong capability and timeline. Dim5 5: every distractor is a real migration path violating exactly one stated constraint.

Argued FOR: D (a managed service) is the strongest case since it hands over the most operation of all, which is what the office said it wanted; loses on the second requirement, keeping the portal's own code. C (containers on a cluster) is the middle rung a consultant would propose. A (VMs) keeps control the office cannot staff. Dim5 5: the ladder is walked from both ends and the key sits at the intersection of two constraints.

Argued FOR: C (each part gets its own data store) is the strongest wrong case - it is a genuine microservices design principle and it even names the coupling the co-op feels; loses because it describes an arrangement rather than what the decomposition buys. B (fewer defects) is a real consequence. A (runs faster) is the common misconception and usually false. Dim5 5: a true design property competing with the purpose is the good-vs-best shape.

Argued FOR: C (autoscaling) is the strongest case because 'requests pile up' reads as a capacity symptom to nearly everyone; loses because the team has confirmed the instance count. A (Kubernetes) is defensible if placement were uneven, and the idle instances show it is not. D (connection limit) is the plausible configuration fix. Dim5 5: the surface points at capacity and the principle is distribution.

Argued FOR: D (neither, clinical systems should never be interruptible) is the strongest wrong case and a real hospital policy position; loses because it also excludes a job that loses nothing on restart. A (both) rests on the overnight window rather than on interruptibility. B (the dispensing job) is contradicted by the stem outright. Dim2 4: B is disarmed by the scenario rather than by the concept. Dim5 4: the restartability contrast is stated plainly.

Argued FOR: B (Cloud Run) is the strongest case for a modernization-minded reader and would be right without the licensing and support terms; loses because the vendor supports the software only while the roaster controls the host. C (GKE) assumes containerization the licence resists. D (replace the software) renegotiates everything. Dim5 4: three constraints all pointing the same way make the mapping direct, but each distractor is a real product decision.

Argued FOR: B (a smaller operations team) is the strongest wrong case because it is stated in business terms and is what boards hear; loses because modernization changes what operations do rather than promising headcount. A (cost optimization) is excluded by the stem. D (faster page load) is a technical improvement dressed as an outcome. Dim2 4: A is eliminated by the stem's own exclusion. Dim5 4.

Argued FOR: A (Cloud Run) is the strongest case for a team that wants less operational work; loses because it removes the node pools and scheduling policy the mill deliberately keeps. B (self-managed Kubernetes on VMs) preserves everything including the one job the team refuses. C (functions) is a re-architecture nobody asked for. Dim5 5: the item turns on where the managed boundary sits, which is exactly the good-vs-best line between GKE and serverless containers.

Re-scored fresh at round 2 after the round-1 overlap bounce; the stem, options and key are unchanged and only rationale.correct was re-expressed. Argued FOR: A (GKE) is the strongest wrong case since a cluster genuinely runs containers and gives the developers their language; loses because configuring and maintaining a cluster is infrastructure management under another name. C (a VM plus a start script) is what two developers often actually do. D (a head-office server) is the pre-cloud default and handles spiky traffic worst. Dim2 4: D is weak next to A. Dim4 5: the re-expressed rationale now argues the boundary in the bank's own words ('takes over everything below the container') and still names the concept's terms. Dim5 4. In the Gate 2 sample as a bounce survivor.

Argued FOR: B (the existing GKE cluster) is the strongest case - the institute already runs one, so marginal cost feels like zero; loses because it brings orchestration the task never needs and someone still operates it. A (a VM kept warm) is the pre-serverless default. D (a nightly batch) is a real design that fails the unpredictable-moment requirement. Dim5 4: run-time, frequency and trigger are all stated, so the mapping is direct.

Argued FOR: C (a nightly copy) is the strongest wrong case operationally and is what most teams would build; loses because it moves data the contract requires to stay put and makes every answer a day old. B (Interconnect) is a real cross-environment product answering connectivity rather than query reach. D (GKE Enterprise) is the same idea for clusters. Dim5 4: 'query the data held on the other provider' points fairly directly at Omni.

Argued FOR: A (copy the data into the new store) is the strongest case because integration usually does involve moving data, and boards hear 'API' as 'feed'; loses because an interface asks the source each time. D (one platform, one store) is the migration reading. C (manage the hardware) is the weakest, though control-system audiences really do hear it that way. Dim2 4: C is thin next to A. Dim5 4: the answer is plain once the concept is held, but the three misreadings are the ones non-technical boards actually hold.

Argued FOR: B (licensed nightly exports under individual contracts) is the strongest wrong case - it does earn money and is what most public bodies do; loses because it stops paying as demand grows, one contract and one file at a time. C (a public search site) serves visitors rather than the businesses asking. A (free download) ends the income with the requests. Dim5 4: 'turn requests into income' cues monetization, but B is a genuinely defensible commercial answer.

Argued FOR: A (Cloud Armor) is the strongest case because opening an interface to hundreds of callers really does raise abuse risk; loses because it issues no credentials, publishes no documentation and meters nothing. D (one shared credential) is what small teams actually ship. B (a second copy of the service) treats a governance problem as capacity. Dim2 4: B is weak. Dim5 4: the requirement list is close to a product feature list.

Argued FOR: D (DDoS) is the strongest wrong case since the visible symptom is slowness and denial-of-service is the reflex diagnosis; loses because a flood installs nothing and stops when it stops. A (ransomware) is defensible as a dormant payload and loses because ransomware exists to be seen. C (misconfiguration) reads spare capacity as self-inflicted exposure. Dim5 5: the surface hands a slowdown and the principle is silent theft of capacity.

Argued FOR: C (retrain the model on harmful instructions) is the strongest wrong case and is a real defence proposal; loses because the poisoned article is still read as legitimate source material. B (harden the infrastructure) is the classical security answer to any breach. D (a platform notice) is a genuine transparency control aimed at the wrong failure. Dim5 5: the attack arrives through content the assistant was designed to trust, which points away from the data layer for most readers.

Argued FOR: A (responsibility passes to the provider) is what many audit committees believe and the reason the question gets asked. B (nothing of substance changes) is the seasoned security lead's scepticism and is half true about obligations. D (physical security stops mattering) is a real misreading of the baseline. Dim5 4: 'what genuinely changes' points at shared responsibility, but each distractor is a position real committees hold.

Argued FOR: A (confidentiality) would hold if anything had been disclosed; B (availability) if the systems had stopped; C (compliance) if an obligation were engaged. Each is a real property of the security model and each is negated by one clause of the stem. Dim2 4: the options are the right family and distinct, but none survives as a live tempter once the stem's three negations are read. Dim5 3: the stem eliminates three properties in order and each option restates its own definition, so a candidate can reach the key by matching negations rather than by holding the concept.

Argued FOR: B (least privilege) is the strongest wrong case and a genuinely good answer to the incident - the contractor's account reached stock records it may not have needed; loses because the trust assumption, not the permission set, is what the lead proposed to change. C (privileged access management) is a real discipline for a narrower account class. D (block contractor devices) is the incident-specific fix that leaves the assumption intact. Dim5 3: the stem states the zero-trust definition almost verbatim ('every request be verified whatever its origin') and then asks for its name.

Argued FOR: A (test monthly) is the strongest wrong case because it takes the criticism seriously and is what most boards fund; loses because more photographs are still photographs. B (publish the certificate) is a real partner-assurance move. D (a stronger firewall) optimizes for the next test. Dim2 4: B and D are thinner than A. Dim5 4: the head of technology's 'photograph rather than a position' framing does part of the work for the candidate.

Argued FOR: A (Sensitive Data Protection) is the strongest wrong case - it is a real product, it is about sensitive data, and buying something is what the board expects; loses because discovery and classification are not encryption. C (a firewall rule) is the network reflex. D (encryption on tagging) is a plausible-sounding conditional. Dim5 5: the item's work is rejecting the board's premise, so the surface points away from the principle.

Argued FOR: C (no further state applies) is the strongest wrong case and the belief most organizations actually hold after covering disk and wire; loses because processing is a recognized third state. A and B are the two states the stem has already cleared. Dim2 4: two of the three options are pre-cleared by the scenario, leaving C as the only live tempter. Dim5 4: C is a genuine misconception, which keeps this above a pure match.

Argued FOR: B (authentication) is the reflex answer for any account-related incident and loses because the credential and the MFA challenge both worked. C (auditing) loses because the logs recorded every step. D (two-step verification) is a sub-case of B and overlaps it rather than adding a distinct pattern. Dim2 4: the three A's are the right family, but D duplicates B's pattern and two options are pre-cleared by the stem. Dim5 3: the stem clears authentication and auditing explicitly and each option carries its own definition, so the key is reachable by elimination on the surface.

Argued FOR: A (faster detection inside the estate) is the strongest wrong case because it is what the team feels it lacks; loses because detection is the security-operations job and the ask was for foresight. B (certification) is assurance about controls. D (a consortium severity index) is invented and sounds standards-like. Dim2 4: D is eliminable on vocabulary. Dim5 4: 'insight into what is coming' points at threat intelligence, though the three-source detail is real content.

Argued FOR: A (Google Security Operations) is the strongest wrong case by construction - it is the right product for the cooperative's second gap, so a reader who does not track which gap is asked about picks it. C (Cloud Logging) is a real step toward that same second gap. D (quarterly manual review) is what many organizations actually do. Dim5 5: the two-gap design means the candidate must hold both product roles, not just recognise one.

Argued FOR: A (the swapped pairing) is the strongest wrong case in the bank's security domain - both named products are correct, only the assignment is reversed, so a candidate with partial recall lands there. B (Model Armor for both) is the over-generalization. C (Cloud Armor plus Security Command Center) is two real products for other jobs. Dim5 5: securing AI versus securing with AI is exactly the good-vs-best distinction.

Argued FOR: A (Cloud Armor) is a real defence for an internet-facing application and loses because it grants no member of staff access. C (Confidential Computing) protects records in use and would be right if the obligation were about processing; it finds none of the copies already in spreadsheets. E (Record Scanner) is invented. Dim2 4: E is eliminable on vocabulary alone. Dim5 4: the two obligations are stated crisply enough to map, though C is a genuine near-miss.

Argued FOR: B (a contractual warranty) is the strongest wrong case and is exactly what an insurer's lawyer would ask for; loses because a warranty allocates consequences if claims are false rather than showing they are true. D (an architecture document) describes design rather than operation. C (a console demonstration) is the vendor speaking with better visuals. Dim5 5: three commercially sensible asks, and the discriminator is independent evidence.

Argued FOR: B (a misconfigured bucket) is the strongest wrong case since exposure is the usual cloud risk story; loses because the contract's concern is a lawful demand, not an unlawful one. A (key strength) is a real control question. D (staff clearance) is a real personnel control. Dim5 4: 'not disclosable to any foreign authority' points at sovereignty, but the security team's report frames the misdirection well.

Argued FOR: A (add electricity, cooling and space) is the strongest wrong case in the domain - it is a real correction to the finance director's comparison and would satisfy most boards; loses because it still omits the people cost and the opportunity cost, which is the completeness the concept is about. B (cash out each year) is a genuine treasury view. C (treat them as equivalent) is the director's own position. Dim5 5: the incomplete-but-improved option is the designed trap and it works.

Argued FOR: B (a monthly report to the deans) is the strongest wrong case because it looks exactly like governance and is what most finance committees adopt; loses because it adds visibility to a university that already has a dashboard and still asks nobody to account. D (a better dashboard) is technology answering a people-and-process question, and the stem says the dashboard already exists. C (fixed equal budgets) is a real but blunt control. Dim5 5.

Argued FOR: C (the organization node) is the strongest wrong case - it is one action, it covers the department, and inheritance works; loses because it binds every other department to a retention rule written for one. A (per project) is explicit and is precisely the work to be avoided. D (a documented standard) is what many trusts actually do. Dim5 4: the two constraints (new projects inherit, others unbound) point squarely at the folder tier.

Argued FOR: B (the swapped pairing) is the strongest wrong case because both named controls are real and only the assignment is wrong. A (budget alerts for both) is the single-instrument answer most finance teams reach for and it detects rather than prevents. C (billing reports) is analysis offered as control. Dim5 5: two problems with different shapes, and the discriminator is prevent-before-spend versus buy-on-the-platform's-terms.

Argued FOR: B (budget threshold rules) is the strongest wrong case since alerts are what most boards associate with cost control; loses because a threshold reports nothing about a quarter that has closed. C (quotas) and D (Spot VMs) both act on future spend, which the stem explicitly rules out. Dim5 4: 'before it decides anything at all' is a clear cue, but the three action-oriented distractors are the real instinct.

Argued FOR: A (Cloud Monitoring) is the strongest wrong case because metrics are where every team starts, and the stem says those dashboards look healthy. D (Cloud Profiler) is the right next question once the slow hop is known. B (Cloud Logging) can reconstruct a journey by hand. Dim5 5: four real observability products, and the discriminator is following one request across services.

Argued FOR: A (more zones) is the strongest wrong case and a genuine resilience improvement; loses because zones are subdivisions of the failure domain the requirement says can be lost. C (more frequent backups) is the classical DR answer that still needs somewhere running. D (publish an SLA) confuses a promise with a capability. Dim5 4: 'if that entire region is lost' is close to handing over the multi-region answer, though A is a real trap for anyone who reads zones as independent.

Argued FOR: A (the reversed order) is the designed trap and catches anyone who knows the three terms but not which binds whom. B (saturation, latency, traffic) is a real vocabulary from the neighbouring golden-signals set. C (all three are objectives) is the flattening misconception. Dim5 4: the three descriptions in the stem are clean, so a candidate holding the definitions maps them directly, but the ordering trap keeps it above recall.
